html:
Liechtenstein became a principality of the Holy Roman Empire on 23 January 1719, when the emperor joined the lordships of Vaduz and Schellenberg under the princely House of Liechtenstein.

The family were rich Austrian nobles, with great estates in Moravia and Bohemia. They bought the two small Alpine lordships so as to own land held directly from the emperor, which gave them a seat in the imperial diet. For more than two centuries the princes lived in Vienna and rarely visited.

The principality outlived the Holy Roman Empire, left the German Confederation when it ended in 1866 and stayed out of both world wars. Prince Franz Joseph II moved to Vaduz Castle in 1938. The family lost its Czech lands after 1945, and the prince still holds more power than any other monarch in western Europe. See Liechtenstein's ties to Switzerland.
sum: Liechtenstein became a principality of the Holy Roman Empire on 23 January 1719, when the emperor joined the lordships of Vaduz and Schellenberg under the princely House of Liechtenstein.
